title: HS2’s tunnel boring machines are halfway to Euston
content: The two machines digging HS2’s tunnels from Old Oak Common are now halfway to Euston, having drilled 2.25 miles of their 4.5-mile journey. The TBM being pushed up to the tunnel starting site in March 2026 (c) HS2 By 17th November, both machines were between West Hampstead and Kilburn High Road stations and are due to finish digging in 2027, stopping underground on the approach to Euston, where HS2’s central London terminus is planned. The machines, named Karen and Madeleine, launched from Old Oak Common in January and March 2026 respectively and work around the clock, advancing about 16 metres a day. As they dig, the machines install precast concrete segments to line the tunnels. The Euston tunnels will require total of 48,294 segments, which are being made in Hartlepool, and the tunnelling is expected to generate about 1.5 million tonnes of excavated material, which is sent back to Old Oak Common, then dispatched by rail for landscaping elsewhere. Inside the Euston tunnel (c) HS2 Once the machines stop, workers will dismantle the TBM and remove most of it back through the completed tunnels. The 8.53-metre-wide cutting heads will be left buried in the ground initially, but when the large Euston cavern is constructed next to the tunnel, it will release the cutting heads for disposal. However, the steel can shields at the front of the machines will be left in place and will form part of the HS2 railway tunnel. That means when HS2 trains arrive or leave Euston station, they will pass through a remaining part of the machine that dug the tunnels. HS2’s chief executive Mark Wild said: “Reaching the halfway mark for building the programme’s last deep bored tunnel is a magnificent achievement by everyone involved. Their work driving the high speed line into central London is fundamental to the long term ambition of increasing the prosperity of the area around Euston. I wish everyone a safe journey to their final destination.” Interactive route map (c) HS2 The tunnel drilling operation is run by HS2’s London tunnelling contractor, the Skanska Costain STRABAG joint venture.
